notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Proverbs 2, drawn from the sources I was able to access. I note the tradition where relevant.

---

## Structure and Overview

The entire chapter is one long conditional sentence in Hebrew (an "alphabetic" poem of 22 verses matching the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet, suggesting completeness — Bruce Waltke, cited at enduringword.com). Verses 1–4 are the "if" (protasis); verses 5–8 and 9–11 form two parallel "then" panels (apodosis); verses 12–19 give specific illustrations of what wisdom rescues from; and verses 20–22 are an antithetic conclusion.

---

## Verses 1–4: The Search for Wisdom

**v. 1 — "My son, if you accept my words and hide my commandments within you"**

- **Traditional reading:** Wisdom begins with *receptivity*. The son must willingly "receive" the father's words and "treasure" (hide/store up) commands internally. David Guzik: "Wisdom can never benefit us if it is not received and treasured." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Matthew Henry:** We must not only receive but *retain* the word, lodging it in our hearts as we do treasures, that it may always be ready. (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)
- **Gill (Reformed Baptist):** Reads this Christologically — the "words" are the doctrines of the Gospel relating to the person, office, and grace of Christ. "Hide my commandments" means in the heart, with high esteem and affection. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** "Hide" = store up (compare v. 4). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Clarke (Methodist tradition, cited by Guzik):** "He who has the rule of his duty only in his Bible and in his head, is not likely to be a steady, consistent character; his heart is not engaged… But he who has the word of God in his heart, works from his heart." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)

**v. 2 — "if you incline your ear to wisdom and direct your heart to understanding"**

- **Traditional reading:** The ear and the heart must both be involved. Inclining the ear suggests attentive listening; applying the heart suggests an intentional, internal effort. Gill: "an inclination of the ear, without an application of the heart … will signify nothing." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/2.htm)
- **David Mathis (Reformed Baptist, Desiring God):** "Wisdom from God is not received with indifference or apathy; it is treasured up. So, for us humans, wisdom begins in the ear and the heart: attentive ears and an inclined heart." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/navigate-the-impossible)
- **Trapp (cited by Guzik):** "Attention of body, intention of mind, and retention of memory, are indispensably desired of all wisdom's scholars." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)

**v. 3 — "if you truly call out to insight and lift your voice to understanding"**

- **Traditional reading:** This is the prayer component. Beyond listening, we must cry out fervently. Gill: "not only attend the ministry of the word by men, but cry to God to give the Spirit of wisdom." Cites James 1:5. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** "Faint desires will not prevail; we must be importunate, as those that know the worth of knowledge and our own want of it… We must cry, as new-born babes, after the sincere milk of the word." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)
- **John Piper (Reformed Baptist):** "Ask for it and really mean it; see James 1:5–7." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/faithfulness-is-improvised)

**v. 4 — "if you seek it like silver and search it out like hidden treasure"**

- **Traditional reading:** This is the climax of the search. Mining and treasure-hunting were arduous, dangerous enterprises (see Job 28). Solomon says wisdom demands that level of effort. G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik): "The way of wisdom is never revealed to triflers." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Poole (cited by Guzik):** "With the same unwearied diligence, and earnest desire, and patient expectation under all delays, disappointments, and difficulties, which worldlings use in the purchase of riches." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Ellicott:** Notes that copper and gold mining was well known long before Solomon (remains found in Sinai and the Bisháree desert). Hiding treasure in the earth was common in the East due to insecurity; hunting lost hoards fascinated Orientals and provides the backdrop for the parable of Matthew 13:44. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **John MacArthur (Dispensational Baptist):** Compares this to Job's description of ancient mining — going deep below the surface "where even the eagle's eye has never gone," down into the waters to mine diamonds, gold, and silver. The pursuit of wisdom demands comparable effort. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/TMU135/pursuing-divine-wisdom)

---

## Verses 5–9: The Reward of Wisdom

**v. 5 — "then you will discern the fear of the LORD and discover the knowledge of God"**

- **Traditional reading:** The reward of diligent seeking is understanding the fear of the Lord — the foundational principle of Proverbs (1:7). Guzik: "without the effort to seek out wisdom, we will lack in our fear of the LORD and knowledge of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Waltke (cited by Guzik):** "'Knowledge of God' refers to personal intimacy with him through obedience to his word (cf. 1 Samuel 3:7)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Ellicott:** Knowing God is "the highest of all gifts, even eternal life itself" (John 17:3). Yet our present knowledge is so imperfect that Paul says it is better expressed by "being known of Him" (Galatians 4:9). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)

**v. 6 — "For the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding"**

- **Traditional reading:** This verse explains *why* seeking wisdom leads to the fear of the Lord: because God is the source. All traditions affirm this. Guzik: "True wisdom is found in Him, and He gives it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Ellicott:** Compares to James 1:5 — God gives "liberally, and upbraideth not." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **David Mathis (Desiring God):** "Real wisdom is from God, given from above, not mustered up but received — not wrestled first from life experience in the world, but coming from him who is above." He further connects this to Colossians 2:3: "In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/navigate-the-impossible)
- **John Piper:** "Jesus is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30)… in him are 'hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge' (Colossians 2:3). To know and love and follow this Jesus is to own the treasure of ultimate and eternal happiness." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/get-wisdom)

**v. 7 — "He stores up sound wisdom for the upright; He is a shield to those who walk with integrity"**

- **Traditional reading:** God both stores up wisdom for the upright and actively protects them. The Hebrew for "sound wisdom" (tushiyyah) is variously rendered.
- **Ellicott:** "Sound wisdom" = literally "furtherance, advancement." Compares Matthew 13:12: "Whosoever hath, unto him shall be given." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Gill:** "Sound wisdom" means "essence, substance… that which really is, and is solid and substantial." He applies it to eternal glory — "an enduring substance" (Proverbs 8:21). The Septuagint renders it "salvation." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** "Wisdom itself, sound wisdom, is laid up for the righteous, laid up in Christ their head, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

**v. 8 — "to guard the paths of justice and protect the way of His saints"**

- **Traditional reading:** God is the guardian of those who walk in justice. Ellicott: "He keepeth the paths of judgment — i.e., protects those who walk in them." Notes that "saints" (chasîdîm) means "ardent worshippers," a term used of the tribe of Levi (Deut. 33:8) and later adopted by the Maccabean faithful (1 Macc. 2:42). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **David Mathis:** Sees a pastoral application: "Our God guards the paths of justice and watches over the way of his saints, and he does so in local churches, through pastor-elders." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/navigate-the-impossible)

**v. 9 — "Then you will discern righteousness and justice and equity—every good path"**

- **Traditional reading:** A second "then" — the fruit of wisdom is not only knowing God but also moral discernment in human relationships. Clarke (cited by Guzik): "He who is taught of God understands the whole law of justice, mercy, righteousness, and truth." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Waltke (cited by Guzik):** "Track (magal) refers to 'cart tracks,' 'wagon ruts.' While the earth is soft, wagon wheels press the trails that others are obliged to follow after it dries and hardens." Wisdom helps us make good "ruts" — habits. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Matthew Henry:** "Those have the best knowledge who know their duty" (Psalm 111:10). (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

---

## Verses 10–11: Wisdom's Internal Work

**v. 10 — "For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge will delight your soul"**

- **Traditional reading:** Wisdom moves from external instruction to internal delight. Garrett (cited by Guzik): "The more wisdom one learns, the more one desires and enjoys it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Trapp (cited by Guzik):** "Spiritual joy mortifies sin. His mouth hankers not after homely provision that hath lately tasted of delicate sustenance." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Matthew Henry:** "When it not only fills the head with notions, but enters into the heart and has a commanding power and influence upon that … when thou callest the practice of virtue, not a slavery and a task, but liberty and pleasure." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

**v. 11 — "Discretion will watch over you, and understanding will guard you"**

- **Traditional reading:** Wisdom now functions as an internal guardian. Guzik: "We need God's protection to gain wisdom (Proverbs 2:7-8), but wisdom also protects us." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Gill:** "Discretion will watch over thee; to keep thee from everything pernicious in doctrine and practice." The Septuagint renders it "good counsel"; the Arabic version, "a just thought shall preserve thee in thy last times." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/2.htm)

---

## Verses 12–15: Deliverance from Evil Men

**v. 12 — "to deliver you from the way of evil, from the man who speaks perversity"**

- **Traditional reading:** Wisdom's first specific rescue is from corrupt companions. Ellicott: "Froward things" (Hebrew tahpûkhôth) = "misrepresentations, distortions of the truth." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** "It will deliver thee from the way of the evil man … and a blessed deliverance it will be, as from the very jaws of death." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

**v. 13 — "from those who leave the straight paths to walk in the ways of darkness"**

- **Traditional reading:** These are apostates — those who knew the right path but abandoned it. Henry: "They leave the paths of uprightness, which they were trained up in and had set out in, shake off the influences of their education … to walk in the ways of darkness." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

**v. 14 — "from those who enjoy doing evil and rejoice in the twistedness of evil"**

- **Traditional reading:** This describes the most advanced stage of moral corruption — taking positive pleasure in evil. Ellicott: "This positive taking pleasure in evil is mentioned by St. Paul (Romans 1:32) as the last stage of degradation." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Waltke (cited by Guzik):** The Hebrew verb for "rejoice" (yagilu) "expresses exuberant, enthusiastic, spontaneous shouts of joy, like those heard in bawdy theaters and bloody stadiums." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)

**v. 15 — "whose paths are crooked and whose ways are devious"**

- **Matthew Henry:** "Their ways are crooked, a great many windings and turnings to escape the pursuit of their convictions … some sly excuse, some subtle evasion." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

---

## Verses 16–19: Deliverance from the Forbidden Woman

**v. 16 — "It will rescue you from the forbidden woman, from the stranger with seductive words"**

- **Traditional reading:** The second specific rescue. Guzik notes the nuance: the Bible does not treat all women as victims; it recognizes the reality of the seductive, immoral woman. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Ellicott:** The two Hebrew terms are zārah ("strange," belonging to another family) and nokhrîyyah ("stranger," belonging to another nation). Suggests Solomon's own marriages to foreign women (1 Kings 11:1) had set a corrupting example in Israel. These women "brought up in the lax views of morality which prevailed among heathen nations … would not consider themselves bound by the high standard of purity which was enjoined upon Hebrew women by the Law." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Kidner (cited by Guzik):** Both terms mean "'one who is outside the circle of [a man's] proper relations, that is, a harlot or an adulteress'." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Clarke (cited by Guzik):** "Hechelikah, she that smooths with her words. The original intimates the glib, oily speeches of a prostitute." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)

**v. 17 — "who abandons the partner of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God"**

- **Traditional reading:** She has a record of disloyalty on two levels — human and divine. Ellicott: "The guide of her youth" = "friend with whom she has lived in intimacy: that is, the husband of her youth." "The covenant of her God" = the marriage covenant made in God's presence (cf. Malachi 2:14, "wife of thy covenant"). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Trapp (cited by Guzik):** "Marriage is a mixed covenant, partly religious and partly civil: the parties tie themselves first to God, and then to one another." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)

**v. 18 — "For her house sinks down to death, and her tracks to the departed spirits"**

- **Traditional reading:** The consequences are lethal. The BSB footnote notes the Hebrew says "Rephaim." Ellicott: The word may signify those "at rest" (Job 3:17) or the "weak" (Isaiah 14:10). He renders: "she sinks down with her house: house and all, like Dathan and Abiram." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Poole (cited by Guzik):** Lists multiple ways her house leads to death: wasting vital spirits, shortening life, dangerous diseases from inordinate lust, the fury of jealous husbands, the sword of civil justice, and "undoubtedly, without repentance, to God's wrath and the second death." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Ross (cited by Guzik):** The "shades" (Rephaim) are "the inhabitants of Sheol … the shadowy continuation of those who have lost their vitality and strength." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)

**v. 19 — "None who go to her return or negotiate the paths of life"**

- **Traditional reading:** This is a true principle, not an absolute promise — Solomon had seen many never return from this path. Guzik: "A life early given to promiscuity and sexual sin is much more difficult to reclaim." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Poole (cited by Guzik):** "Adulterers and whoremongers are very rarely brought to repentance, but are generally hardened by the power and deceitfulness of that lust, and by God's just judgment, peculiarly inflicted upon such persons." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Matthew Henry:** "It is very rare that any who are caught in this snare of the devil recover themselves, so much is the heart hardened, and the mind blinded, by the deceitfulness of this sin." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

---

## Verses 20–22: The Two Destinies

**v. 20 — "So you will follow in the ways of the good, and keep to the paths of the righteous"**

- **Traditional reading:** The positive purpose of wisdom — not merely to avoid evil but to walk in the good path. Henry: "We must avoid the way of the evil man, and the strange woman, in order that we may walk in good ways; we must cease to do evil, in order that we may learn to do well." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)
- **Wiersbe (cited by Guzik):** Outlines chapter 2 as three walks: walking with God (vv. 1–9), walking with the wicked (vv. 10–19), walking with the righteous (vv. 20–22). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)

**v. 21 — "For the upright will inhabit the land, and the blameless will remain in it"**

- **Traditional reading:** Under the Mosaic covenant, this promised inheritance in Canaan. Ellicott: "The upright shall dwell in the land — i.e., of Canaan, according to the old promise made to Abraham, renewed in the fifth commandment." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm)
- **Trapp (cited by Guzik):** "Here the wise man speaks after the manner of Moses' law, under which he lived; Deuteronomy 11:8." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Matthew Henry** extends it typologically: "They shall dwell and remain for ever in the heavenly Canaan, of which the earthly one was but a type." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

**v. 22 — "but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the unfaithful will be uprooted"**

- **Traditional reading:** The stark alternative. Waltke (cited by Guzik): "Here the wicked will be cut off because they defile the earth and threaten the relationship of the righteous with their God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
- **Matthew Henry:** "They think to take root in it, but they and their families shall be rooted out of it … There is a day coming which shall leave them neither root nor branch, Malachi 4:1." (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

---

## Distinctive Readings by Tradition

### The "Strange Woman" as Spiritual Adultery (Anglican / older commentators)

Ellicott reports that "commentators have very generally found in it a spiritual meaning, a warning against idolatry and apostasy." He notes that Jeremiah 3:4 borrows the very phrase "guide of her youth" to reprove Israel's faithlessness, and the marriage-as-covenant figure runs through the prophets and into the New Testament (Christ and the Church). Matthew Henry likewise acknowledges this figurative reading: "Many learned interpreters think that this caution against the strange woman … is to be understood figuratively, as a caution … against idolatry, which is spiritual whoredom." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/2.htm) (https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC20002.HTM)

### Christological Reading (Reformed Baptist — Gill)

John Gill reads the entire chapter through the lens of Gospel revelation. "My words" = the doctrines of the Gospel; "wisdom" = Christ; "knowledge of God" = found only in the Gospel, "not by the light of nature … no, nor in the law of Moses." For Gill, the "sound wisdom" laid up is the fullness of grace in Christ, and the "strange woman" represents not only literal immorality but false doctrine. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/2.htm)

### Christ as the Treasure (Reformed Baptist — Piper)

John Piper connects v. 4 directly to Colossians 2:3: "In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." He concludes: "The command, 'Get wisdom,' means first and foremost 'Come to Jesus! Come to Jesus!' in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/get-wisdom)

### Word + Spirit Emphasis (Reformed Baptist — David Mathis, Desiring God)

David Mathis emphasizes the dual dynamic: wisdom comes "from his mouth" (God's written Word) but also must be sought in dependent prayer ("call out … raise your voice"). He draws a parallel to Proverbs 1:20-33 where Wisdom calls out; here the wise not only hear but *call out themselves*. This reflects the Reformed accent on the necessity of both Scripture and the Spirit's illumination. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/navigate-the-impossible)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (David Guzik, Enduring Word)

While largely consistent with evangelical readings, Guzik's commentary reflects charismatic emphasis in its practical application style and its strong stress on the active, personal involvement of God as shield and protector in the believer's daily life. Guzik also emphasizes that wisdom becomes a "self-perpetuating protection — the more we desire it, the more it keeps us from making decisions that bring regret," reflecting a transformational/spiritual-formation accent. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship — Hebrew Acrostic Structure

Proverbs 2 is a single 22-verse acrostic sentence matching the Hebrew alphabet. Waltke (cited by Guzik): "probably to suggest its completeness." This literary observation is widely accepted across traditions and does not affect doctrinal reading. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)

### The "Rephaim" in Verse 18

The Hebrew reads "Rephaim" (BSB footnote). NET Bible notes and modern scholarship identify these as the shadowy inhabitants of the underworld, not "giants" as some older translations rendered it. Ross (cited by Guzik): "The 'shades' are the inhabitants of Sheol; the term describes the shadowy continuation of those who have lost their vitality and strength." This reflects the broader ancient Near Eastern conception of the afterlife as a dim, shadowy existence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-2/)
